title: Cap. X Arg. VII open: Arminius’s three decrees leave church-acquisition to free will; Grevinchovius and Episcopius admit redemption may apply to none / church may wholly fail
pass_a_gloss: If, as Arminius lays down, after God’s decree of giving Christ as Mediator and Saviour, and that other by which he decreed to make safe whomsoever under the condition of repentance, faith, and perseverance, and likewise also that third by which he decreed to administer unto all the means necessary unto repentance and faith; if, I say, these three decrees being laid down, the election and reprobation of singular persons, salvation and damnation, depend from foresight of men’s faith or unbelief, then it follows that it was left unto men’s free will that they could utterly evacuate the end of the Lord’s passion, that is, the acquisition of the Church: So that, that Christ was not dead in vain, that he has a Church of elect efficaciously redeemed by his blood, would have come about not from some antecedent decree, or special grace of God electing certain members unto Christ the Head and predestining them to be quickened and saved through Christ, but from the contingent operation of human wills. For all mortals, if they be considered as not yet elect, nor predetermined by that special providence of God which we call Predestination unto having faith and persevering in the same, can remain in their unbelief, can spring back from faith once received, can, in a word, fall from salvation, and leave Christ the Redeemer altogether without a redeemed Church. They cannot deny this consequence who try to fetch election and reprobation from foresight of faith and unbelief. Grevinchovius therefore candidly admitted it, Dissert. De morte Christi, pag. 14. We assert, he says, that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none because of the intervening unbelief of all. So also Episcopius, resting on this Arminian principle, confesses that the whole Church on earth can fail, and that it is not necessary, for Christ to remain King and Head, that he always have some true Church on earth.
pass_b_english: If, as Arminius sets it, after God’s decree to give Christ as Mediator and Savior, and the second decree to save any under the condition of repentance, faith, and perseverance, and the third to administer to all the means needed for repentance and faith—if, with those three decrees in place, election and reprobation of singular persons, salvation and damnation, hang on foresight of men’s faith or unbelief—then it follows that free will was left able to empty out the end of the Lord’s passion, the acquiring of the Church. So that Christ not dying in vain, and having a church of elect efficaciously redeemed by his blood, would come not from some antecedent decree or special grace of God electing certain members to Christ the Head and predestining them to be made alive and saved through him, but from the contingent working of human wills. For all mortals, if taken as not yet elect and not predetermined by that special providence we call Predestination to have faith and persevere in it, can stay in unbelief, spring back from faith once received, in a word fall from salvation and leave Christ the Redeemer with no redeemed church at all. Those who fetch election and reprobation from foresight of faith and unbelief cannot deny this consequence. Grevinchovius admitted it candidly (Dissert. De morte Christi, p. 14): We assert that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none because of the intervening unbelief of all. So Episcopius, resting on this Arminian principle, confesses the whole church on earth can fail, and that Christ need not always have some true church on earth in order to remain King and Head.
source_text: Si, ut ponit Arminius, post decretum Dei de dando Christo Mediatore et Salvatore, et illud alterum quo decrevit quosvis sub conditione resipiscentiae, fidei et perseverantiae salvos facere, itemque et illud tertium quo decrevit media ad resipiscentiam et fidem necessaria omnibus administrare; si, inquam, positis hisce tribus decretis, singularium personarum electio et reprobatio, salus et damnatio dependeat ex praevisa hominum sive fide sive infidelitate, tum sequitur, hominum libero arbitrio relictum fuisse, ut possent finem Dominicae passionis, hoc est, acquisitionem Ecclesiae, prorsus evacuare: Ita ut, quod Christus frustra mortuus non fuerit, quod habeat Ecclesiam electorum sanguine suo efficaciter redemptam, non ex antecedaneo aliquo decreto, aut speciali gratia Dei membra quaedam Christo Capiti eligentis et per Christum vivificanda et salvanda praedestinantis, sed ex contingente operatione humanarum voluntatum evenerit. Universi enim mortales, si considerentur ut nondum electi, nec speciali illa providentia Dei, quam Praedestinationem vocamus, ad habendam fidem et perseverandum in eadem praedeterminati, possunt in sua incredulitate manere, possunt a fide suscepta resilire, possunt, uno verbo, a salute excidere, et Christum Redemptorem, absque Ecclesia redempta prorsus relinquere. Hanc consequentiam non possunt negare, qui electionem et reprobationem ex praevisione fidei et infidelitatis conantur arcessere. Ingenue itaque illam admisit Grevinchovius, Dissert. De morte Christi, pag. 14. Asserimus, inquit, potuisse omnibus impetratam esse redemptionem, et tamen nullis applicatam propter intervenientem omnium infidelitatem. Sic etiam Episcopius hoc principio Arminiano innixus, fatetur totam Ecclesiam in terris deficere posse, neque necesse esse ad hoc, ut Christus Rex et Caput maneat, illum habere semper Ecclesiam aliquam veram in terris.
